question: Arrange the haloacetic acids
explanation: pKa: FCH2COOH 2.66 < ClCH2COOH 2.86 < BrCH2COOH 2.90 < ICH2COOH 3.18 < CH3COOH 4.76. -I effect falls F > Cl > Br > I.
trap: Do not use size/polarisability of the halogen; only the -I effect matters here.

question: Arrange the chloroacetic acids
explanation: pKa: 0.65 < 1.29 < 2.86 < 4.76. Each extra Cl adds -I effect and stabilises the carboxylate.

question: Arrange the chlorobutanoic acids
explanation: pKa: 2-Cl 2.84 < 3-Cl 4.06 < 4-Cl 4.52 < butanoic 4.82. The -I effect decays rapidly with distance from COOH.
trap: The 4-chloro acid is still stronger than butanoic acid, only slightly.

question: Arrange the following
explanation: Approx. pKa: CH3COOH 4.8, phenol 10, H2O 15.7, EtOH 16, HC≡CH 25. Carboxylate and phenoxide are resonance stabilised; alkoxide is destabilised by +I of R; sp carbanion is stabilised by 50% s-character.
trap: Water is more acidic than ethanol; alkyl groups destabilise the alkoxide.

question: Arrange the alcohols in solution
explanation: pKa: 15.5, 16, 17, 18. +I of alkyl groups intensifies negative charge on O and alkoxide is less solvated when bulky.
trap: In the gas phase the order reverses because polarisable alkyl groups stabilise the anion.

question: Arrange the phenols
explanation: pKa: picric acid 0.4, 2,4-dinitrophenol 4.1, p-nitrophenol 7.15, phenol 10. Each NO2 at o/p gives -I and -R stabilisation of the phenoxide.
trap: Picric acid is as strong as a mineral acid; it dissolves in NaHCO3.

question: Arrange the benzoic acids
explanation: pKa: o-nitro 2.17 < benzoic 4.20 < p-methyl 4.34 < p-methoxy 4.47. Ortho effect strengthens o-nitro acid; +I/+R groups weaken acid.

question: Arrange the carbon acids (acidity of the most acidic C–H)
explanation: pKa: acetylacetone 9, ethyl acetoacetate 10.7, diethyl malonate 13, acetone 19. Two C=O groups stabilise the enolate; ketone C=O is a better acceptor than ester C=O (ester carbonyl is donated by OR).

question: Arrange the following C–H acids
explanation: pKa: nitromethane 10, acetone 19, ethyne 25, ethane 50. Nitronate and enolate are resonance stabilised (NO2 better); sp carbanion is stabilised by s-character.

question: If a nitro group is introduced at the para position of phenol, the acidic strength
explanation: p-Nitrophenol (pKa 7.15) is stronger than phenol (10). The -R and -I effects of NO2 stabilise the phenoxide ion.

question: If a methoxy group is introduced at the meta position of benzoic acid, the acidic strength
explanation: m-Methoxybenzoic acid pKa 4.09 < benzoic acid 4.20. At meta, +R does not operate, so only -I of OMe acts and strengthens the acid.
trap: p-OCH3 weakens the acid (4.47) because +R wins at para.

question: If a methoxy group is introduced at the para position of benzoic acid, the acidic strength
explanation: p-Methoxybenzoic acid pKa 4.47 > 4.20. +R of OMe at para outweighs -I and destabilises the carboxylate.

question: If a methyl group is introduced at the alpha carbon of acetic acid (giving propanoic acid), the acidic strength
explanation: +I effect of CH3 destabilises the carboxylate; pKa rises 4.76 to 4.87.

question: If a nitro group is introduced at the meta position of phenol, the acidic strength
explanation: m-Nitrophenol (8.4) is stronger than phenol (10) through -I only; it is weaker than the para isomer (7.15) because -R is absent.

question: Which is the stronger first acid (pKa1): maleic acid or fumaric acid?
explanation: pKa1: maleic 1.9, fumaric 3.0, since the maleate monoanion is stabilised by intramolecular H-bond. For the second step fumaric is stronger (pKa2 4.4 vs 6.1).
trap: Ranking reverses for the second dissociation.

question: Compare the acidity of phenol and cyclohexanol
explanation: Phenol pKa 10 vs cyclohexanol ~16-18; phenoxide is resonance stabilised, cyclohexoxide is not.

question: Which of the following dissolves in aqueous NaOH but not in aqueous NaHCO3?
explanation: NaHCO3 reacts only with acids stronger than H2CO3 (pKa 6.4). Phenol (pKa 10) is weaker; carboxylic acids and picric acid (0.4) are stronger.

question: Among the following hydrocarbons, the most acidic is
explanation: Cyclopentadiene (pKa 16) gives the aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion (6 pi electrons). Cycloheptatriene gives an antiaromatic-leaning, non-planar anion (pKa 36).

question: Which is the strongest acid?
explanation: Ortho effect: any ortho substituent twists COOH out of the ring plane, removing its resonance with the ring, increasing acidity. pKa: ortho 2.17, meta 3.45, para 3.44, H 4.20.
trap: Ortho-substituted benzoic acids are stronger than benzoic acid regardless of whether the group is donating or withdrawing.

question: Arrange the following (aqueous solution)
criterion: decreasing order of basic strength in aqueous solution
explanation: pKa of conjugate acids: 10.73, 10.62, 9.80, 9.25. +I effect, offset by poorer solvation of the 3° ammonium ion.

question: Arrange the following ethylamines (aqueous solution)
criterion: decreasing order of basic strength in aqueous solution
explanation: pKa of conjugate acids: 11.09, 10.75, 10.65, 9.25. Bulkier ethyl groups keep 3° in between: 2° > 3° > 1° > NH3.
trap: The ethyl order differs from the methyl order (3° > 1° here).

question: Arrange the methylamines in the gas phase
explanation: Without solvation, only +I/polarisability of alkyl groups acts: 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3.

question: Arrange the following
explanation: pKaH: 10.6, 9.25, 4.6, 0.8. N lone pair in aniline is delocalised into the ring; diphenylamine delocalises into two rings.

question: Arrange the anilines
explanation: pKaH: 5.1, 4.6, 4.0, 1.0. +I/hyperconjugation of CH3 increases electron density at N; Cl is -I; NO2 is -I and -R.

question: Arrange the following nitrogen bases
explanation: pKaH: piperidine 11.1 (sp3 N), pyridine 5.2 (sp2 N), aniline 4.6, pyrrole -3.8. Pyrrole's lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet.

question: Arrange the following
explanation: Basicity falls with increasing s-character of the N lone pair orbital: sp3 > sp2 > sp.

question: Arrange the pyridines
explanation: pKaH: DMAP 9.6, 4-aminopyridine 9.2, pyridine 5.2, 4-nitropyridine 1.6. The +R NR2 group delocalises into the ring N; NO2 withdraws.

question: Arrange the following
explanation: pKaH: guanidine 13.6, methylamine 10.6, pyridine 5.2, acetamide about -0.5. Guanidinium is a symmetric, resonance-stabilised cation.

question: Arrange the following anions
explanation: Basicity follows the pKa of the conjugate acid: t-BuOH 18, EtOH 16, PhOH 10, AcOH 4.8.

question: Arrange the nitroanilines
explanation: pKaH: aniline 4.6, m-nitro 2.5, p-nitro 1.0, o-nitro -0.3. At meta only -I acts; at p/o -R also acts; ortho adds proximity and H-bonding to the neutral amine.

question: If a nitro group is introduced at the para position of aniline, the basic strength
explanation: pKaH falls from 4.6 to 1.0. NO2 withdraws by -I and -R, reducing availability of the N lone pair.

question: If a methoxy group is introduced at the para position of aniline, the basic strength
explanation: p-Anisidine pKaH 5.34 > 4.6. +R of OMe at para increases electron density on N.

question: If a methyl group is introduced at the ortho position of aniline, the basic strength
explanation: o-Toluidine pKaH 4.4 < aniline 4.6, whereas p-toluidine is 5.1. Ortho effect: steric hindrance to solvation/protonation of NH3+ lowers basicity for essentially every ortho group.
trap: Despite +I of CH3, the ortho isomer is weaker than aniline.

question: If the nitrogen of aniline is acetylated (giving acetanilide), the basic strength
explanation: N lone pair is delocalised into the C=O as well as the ring; acetanilide is essentially non-basic.

question: If a fluorine atom is introduced at the beta carbon of ethylamine (giving 2-fluoroethylamine), the basic strength
explanation: -I effect of F reduces electron density on N; pKaH ~9.0 vs 10.65.

question: Which is more basic: pyridine or pyrrole?
explanation: Pyridine's sp2 lone pair lies in the plane and is free; in pyrrole the lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet and protonation destroys aromaticity.

question: Which is more basic: piperidine or pyridine?
explanation: sp3 lone pair (pKaH 11.1) vs sp2 lone pair (5.2); higher s-character holds lone pair tighter.

question: Which is the stronger base: 1,8-bis(dimethylamino)naphthalene (proton sponge) or N,N-dimethylaniline?
explanation: pKaH 12.1 vs 5.1. In the sponge, NMe2 groups are held close, so lone-pair repulsion and strain are relieved on protonation, and the cation is stabilised by a strong N-H...N bond.

question: Guanidine is a very strong organic base (pKaH ~13.6) because
options: its N atoms are sp3 hybridised
its conjugate acid is stabilised by delocalisation of the positive charge over three N atoms
explanation: Protonation at imine N gives the guanidinium ion, a symmetrical, resonance-stabilised cation with Y-delocalisation.

question: The exceptional basicity of proton sponge (pKaH ~12) is due to
options: +I effect of two methyl groups only
release of steric strain between NMe2 groups and strong intramolecular N-H...N hydrogen bond in conjugate acid
explanation: Peri NMe2 groups repel in the neutral form (lone pairs, twisted); protonation relieves this and forms a short H-bond.

question: In the gas phase the most basic of the methylamines is
explanation: Without solvation, each CH3 group stabilises the ammonium ion by +I and polarisation, so 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3. In water 3° falls below 2°/1° because its ion is less H-bonded.

question: Arrange the chlorophenols and phenol
explanation: pKa: o 8.5, m 9.1, p 9.4, phenol 10.0. -I dominates and decays with distance; +R at o/p reduces the effect slightly at para.
trap: Halogens: -I wins overall, so all are stronger than phenol.

question: Arrange the hydroxybenzoic acids and benzoic acid
explanation: pKa: ortho 2.98, meta 4.08, benzoic 4.20, para 4.58. Ortho: H-bond and ortho effect; meta: -I only; para: +R dominates.

question: Which is the stronger acid: m-methoxybenzoic acid or p-methoxybenzoic acid?
explanation: pKa 4.09 vs 4.47. Meta: -I only; para: +R opposes -I.

question: Which is the stronger acid: p-nitrophenol or m-nitrophenol?
explanation: pKa 7.15 vs 8.4. At para, NO2 exerts both -I and -R; at meta only -I.

question: Which is the stronger acid: 4-nitrophenol or 3,5-dimethyl-4-nitrophenol?
explanation: pKa 7.15 vs 8.25. Two flanking methyls twist the NO2 out of the plane (steric inhibition of resonance), cancelling its -R effect.
trap: The methyls are meta to OH, yet the SIR effect weakens the acid.

question: If any substituent (e.g. CH3) is introduced at the ortho position of benzoic acid, the acidic strength
explanation: Ortho effect: o-toluic acid pKa 3.91 < benzoic 4.20. Steric twisting of COOH out of the ring plane reduces its resonance with the ring and raises acidity.
trap: Applies even to electron-donating ortho groups.

question: If a nitro group is introduced at the meta position of benzoic acid, the acidic strength
explanation: m-Nitrobenzoic acid pKa 3.45 < 4.20. -I effect stabilises the carboxylate.

question: p-Hydroxybenzoic acid is a weaker acid than benzoic acid because
options: -I effect of OH at para dominates
+R effect of OH at para outweighs its -I effect
explanation: At para, +R dominates (pKa 4.58 vs 4.20); at meta, only -I acts (4.08).

question: Which has the higher enol content: acetylacetone or ethyl acetoacetate?
explanation: About 80% vs 8% (neat liquid). Ketone C=O is a stronger H-bond acceptor and conjugates better than ester C=O.

question: In water, which has the higher enol content: cyclohexane-1,3-dione or acetylacetone?
explanation: Cyclohexane-1,3-dione is predominantly enolic in polar solvents (enol is polar and strongly H-bonded to water); the ring holds the diketone s-cis (unfavourable dipoles), so the enol is preferred. Acetylacetone is only about 15% enol in water.
trap: Acetylacetone's own enol content is highest in non-polar solvents because of the chelated cis-enol.

question: If the solvent is changed from hexane to water for acetylacetone, its enol content
explanation: Intramolecular H-bond in the enol is strongest in non-polar solvents (~92% enol in hexane); water H-bonds to the keto C=O and the more polar diketo form, so enol content drops to ~15%.

question: If a second carbonyl group is introduced at the beta position of acetone (giving acetylacetone), the enol content
explanation: Enol content rises from about 10^-4 % to ~80% through conjugation and intramolecular H-bonding.

question: Which of the following does NOT show keto-enol tautomerism?
explanation: Benzophenone has no alpha-hydrogen on a carbon adjacent to the carbonyl.

question: The high enol content of acetylacetone is attributed to
options: conjugation and a strong intramolecular hydrogen bond (six-membered chelate ring)
explanation: The cis-enol forms a conjugated six-membered ring with O-H...O chelation.

question: Arrange the methyl halides
explanation: mu: CH3Cl 1.87 D, CH3F 1.85, CH3Br 1.81, CH3I 1.62. Dipole = charge x distance: F is most electronegative but C-F bond is short.
trap: CH3F does not have the highest dipole moment.

question: Arrange the carbon-carbon bonds
explanation: 1.54, 1.47, 1.39, 1.34 angstrom. The central bond of butadiene has partial double-bond character (sp2-sp2).

question: Which has the higher boiling point: o-nitrophenol or p-nitrophenol?
explanation: bp: ortho 216, para 279 degC. Ortho has intramolecular H-bond (chelation), so it is steam volatile; para has intermolecular H-bonds.
trap: Ortho is the one that steam distils.

question: Which has the larger dipole moment: cis-1,2-dichloroethene or trans-1,2-dichloroethene?
explanation: Cis: bond dipoles add (1.9 D); trans: they cancel (0 D).

question: Which has the higher boiling point: cis-but-2-ene or trans-but-2-ene?
explanation: bp: cis 3.7, trans 0.9 degC. Cis has a net dipole; trans packs better into the crystal and has the higher melting point.
trap: Melting point trend is opposite (trans higher).

question: o-Nitrophenol is steam volatile and has a lower boiling point than its isomers because
options: it has a higher molar mass
explanation: Chelation between OH and NO2 prevents intermolecular association.

question: In benzene, all C-C bond lengths are 1.39 angstrom, intermediate between
explanation: Resonance gives bond order 1.5: between C-C single (1.54) and C=C (1.34).

question: If the nitro group of nitrophenol is moved from the para to the ortho position, the volatility
explanation: Ortho has intramolecular H-bonding; para has intermolecular H-bonding, so ortho is more volatile.
